findings.summary: PPTX export aborts the whole download if any single image fetch fails, unlike the PDF path which degrades to a blank placeholder
findings.evidence: `fetchImage: async (src) => { const blob = await docsImageFetcher(src); ... }` (pptx-actions.ts:93-99) lets any rejection propagate. `docsImageFetcher` (export-utils.ts:46-56) throws on any non-OK response (404 deleted image, or 401 after the JWT cookie expires — it uses plain `fetch`, not `fetchWithAuth`, so there is no refresh retry). In `exportPptx` the fetch loop is unguarded: `const { bytes, mime } = await opts.fetchImage(src);` (packages/slides/src/export/pptx/index.ts:162). The PDF path deliberately tolerates this: `resolveDeckImages` wraps the fetch in try/catch and substitutes BLANK_PNG (packages/slides/src/export/pdf.ts:277-282). Result: a deck containing one broken/inaccessible image can never be exported to PPTX — the user only sees "Export failed: Image fetch failed: 404".

mergedFrom.summary: Empty deck: PPTX export produces a slide-less archive where the PDF path explicitly errors
mergedFrom.evidence: `exportSlidesPdf` guards with `if (doc.slides.length === 0) throw new Error('Cannot export an empty presentation to PDF.')` (packages/slides/src/export/pdf.ts:103-105). `exportPptx` has no such guard (packages/slides/src/export/pptx/index.ts:130-146; the slide loop at 274 simply runs zero times), so `exportSlidesPptxAndDownload` downloads a .pptx with no slides and reports success (`onProgress(0,0)` also suppresses the toast, export-utils.ts:134). PowerPoint may treat a slide-less presentation as needing repair.

findings.summary: `blob.type || "image/png"` can label non-PNG bytes as PNG, producing a media part with the wrong extension/content-type
findings.evidence: `mime: blob.type || "image/png"` — a backend image served with no Content-Type (blob.type === "") or with `application/octet-stream` yields "image/png"/octet-stream, and `extFromMime` falls back to `'png'` for anything unrecognised (packages/slides/src/export/pptx/index.ts:95-96). JPEG/GIF bytes then get written to `ppt/media/imageN.png` with the PNG Default content type, which PowerPoint may reject (repair prompt) or fail to render. Sniffing the byte magic, or at least propagating the element's known mime, would avoid this.

findings.summary: New PPTX export fetches arbitrary, document-controlled image URLs with `credentials: "include"` and no scheme/host allowlist
findings.evidence:
`exportSlidesPptxAndDownload` passes every image element's `src` straight into `docsImageFetcher` (pptx-actions.ts:93-99), which resolves it via `resolveImageUrl` — that function deliberately preserves ANY absolute URL (`export-utils.ts:15`) — and then issues `fetch(resolved, { credentials: "include" })` (export-utils.ts:51).

The `src` is fully attacker-controllable: the v1 content endpoint validates only `id`/`type`/`frame` per element (`packages/backend/src/api/v1/docs-content.controller.ts:337-357`) and never inspects `data.src`, so any workspace member or API-key holder (or a collaborator driving a patched CRDT client on a shared deck) can store `data: { src: "https://attacker.example/beacon.png" }`.

Attack: attacker plants such an element in a shared deck; when a victim clicks Export → PowerPoint (slides-export-button.tsx), the victim's browser performs a credentialed GET to the attacker origin — leaking victim IP/UA/export timing, performing GET-side-effect CSRF against third-party or intranet origins with the victim's ambient cookies (no preflight for a simple GET, so the request is sent even when the response is CORS-blocked), and, when the attacker server returns permissive CORS headers, embedding arbitrary attacker bytes verbatim as a `ppt/media/` part in the victim's downloaded file. Same pattern exists in the pre-existing PDF/DOCX paths, but this change adds a third unguarded consumer and the PPTX one embeds the fetched bytes byte-for-byte rather than rasterising them.

findings.summary: No size or content-type validation on bytes fetched for PPTX media parts
findings.evidence: `await blob.arrayBuffer()` is called on an unbounded response and `mime` falls back to `blob.type || "image/png"`; `exportPptx` then writes those bytes as `ppt/media/imageN.<ext>` (packages/slides/src/export/pptx/index.ts:161-166). A hostile or oversized `src` (attacker-controlled, see the credentialed-fetch finding) can therefore exhaust the exporting tab's memory or place non-image content into the archive the victim then shares onward. No `Content-Length`/max-bytes check or MIME allowlist exists on this path.
searchedFor: read packages/frontend/src/app/slides/pdf-actions.ts for a comparable size guard

findings.summary: safeFilename (now also used for .pptx) does not strip control characters or Unicode bidi-override chars from the attacker-influenceable title
findings.evidence: The sanitiser only removes `\ / : * ? " < > |`. A deck title is editable by any collaborator on a shared document, and the title flows into `safeFilename(title, "pptx")` → `a.download` (export-utils.ts:61-71). A title containing U+202E (RTL override) or C0 control characters survives sanitisation, letting a malicious collaborator control how the downloaded filename renders in the victim's download manager/file browser (classic extension-spoofing presentation attack). Hardening: also strip `[�-‎‏‪-‮⁦-⁩]` and leading dots.

findings.summary: New datasources doc advertises an SSL toggle, but the client disables TLS certificate verification (`rejectUnauthorized: false`)
findings.evidence: `packages/documentation/sheets/datasources.md` (added by this change) tells users to enable **SSL** "if your database requires it", presenting it as a protection. The implementation builds the pg client with `ssl: ds.sslEnabled ? { rejectUnauthorized: false } : false` (datasource.service.ts:204), so the server certificate is never validated — an on-path attacker between the Wafflebase backend and the customer database can transparently MITM the connection and capture the decrypted database username/password (decrypt() is called on the same line). The new documentation makes the false assurance user-facing. Pre-existing code, surfaced by the doc added here.

findings.summary: New datasources doc promises read-only query execution, enforced only by a keyword denylist that is bypassable
findings.evidence: `sheets/datasources.md` (added here) states the results grid is read-only and implies queries are read-only. Enforcement is a regex denylist (`INSERT|UPDATE|DELETE|DROP|ALTER|CREATE|TRUNCATE|GRANT|REVOKE|EXEC|EXECUTE`) plus a first-token check for SELECT/WITH (sql-validator.ts:38-57). `SELECT ... INTO newtable FROM t` starts with SELECT and contains no denylisted keyword, so it passes and writes to the target database; the semicolon splitter strips only single-quoted strings (line 60), so dollar-quoted bodies (`$$ ... ; ... $$`) also evade the multi-statement check. Any workspace member — not just the datasource owner, see datasource.controller.ts:133-145 where only `assertMember` is required — can send these through `POST /datasources/:id/query` using credentials they never possessed. Pre-existing code newly advertised by this change; I did not execute a live bypass, hence low confidence.

findings.summary: DataSource create/update responses return the stored (encrypted) password field, unlike the masked read paths
findings.evidence: `findAllByWorkspace` (line 66-69) and `findOne` (line 77) explicitly mask `password: '********'`, but `create` (line 44) and `update` (line 95) return the raw Prisma record, which includes the `encrypt(dto.password)` ciphertext, to any workspace member calling those endpoints. Leaking ciphertext plus IV to lower-privileged members enables offline attack if the encryption key is ever exposed and breaks the masking invariant the read paths establish. Out of diff; surfaced while verifying the datasource documentation added here.

findings.summary: GET /images/:id has no auth guard — workspace images are readable by anyone holding the id
findings.evidence: `upload` and `delete` are `@UseGuards(JwtAuthGuard)` but `get` (line 44-53) is unauthenticated and serves any object whose id matches `VALID_IMAGE_ID_PATTERN` (a UUID + extension), with `Cache-Control: public, immutable`. Confidentiality rests entirely on UUID unguessability, not on workspace membership. The PPTX export added here fetches these URLs credentialed (export-utils.ts:51) — a comment in pptx-actions.ts:80 asserts "backend images are same-origin-fetched with cookies", implying an authorization that the endpoint does not actually perform. Pre-existing; flagged because the new export path depends on the assumption.

+# Import & Export
+
+Wafflebase reads and writes the file formats your team already uses, so you
+can bring existing work in and take finished work out. Nothing is locked to
+the platform.
+
+## At a glance
+
+| Product | Import | Export |
+|---------|--------|--------|
+| **Sheets** | Excel (`.xlsx`) | — *(CSV/JSON via [CLI](../developers/cli))* |
+| **Docs** | Word (`.docx`) | Word (`.docx`), PDF (`.pdf`) |
+| **Slides** | PowerPoint (`.pptx`) | PowerPoint (`.pptx`), PDF (`.pdf`) |
+
+Import always creates a **new** document; it never overwrites an open one.
+Export downloads a file from the document you are editing.
+
+## Importing files
+
+From your workspace, open the **New** menu and choose an import option:
+
+- **Import XLSX** — creates a new spreadsheet from an Excel workbook. Each
+  sheet in the workbook becomes a tab. Values, formulas, and basic cell
+  formatting are brought across.
+- **Import DOCX** — creates a new document from a Word file, mapping
+  paragraphs, headings, lists, tables, and inline formatting into the editor.
+- **Import PPTX** — creates a new deck from a PowerPoint file: slides,
+  text boxes, shapes, images, tables, and theme colors are converted to
+  native Wafflebase elements.
+
+Large files show a progress indicator while they are parsed and any embedded
+images are uploaded into your workspace.
+
+## Exporting files
+
+### Docs
+
+In the document editor, open the **Export** menu (the download icon in the
+header) and choose:
+
+- **Word (`.docx`)** — the full document, including tables and headers/footers.
+- **PDF (`.pdf`)** — a paginated, print-ready PDF that mirrors the on-screen
+  page layout.
+
+### Slides
+
+In the presentation editor, open the **Export** menu and choose:
+
+- **PowerPoint (`.pptx`)** — an editable deck with slides, shapes, text,
+  images, tables, and the theme preserved as DrawingML.
+- **PDF (`.pdf`)** — one slide per page, ready to share or print.
+
+### Sheets
+
+Spreadsheets export to CSV or JSON through the
+[command-line tool](../developers/cli) (`wafflebase sheets …`). A built-in
+download menu in the grid editor is on the roadmap.
+
+## Fidelity notes
+
+Wafflebase aims for a faithful round-trip, but the source formats are large
+and some constructs have no exact equivalent:
+
+- **PPTX/DOCX import is best-effort.** Common content — text, lists, tables,
+  shapes, images, and theme colors — converts cleanly. Rare or
+  application-specific features (embedded objects, macros, exotic effects) may
+  be simplified or dropped.
+- **Fonts** referenced by an imported file must be available in Wafflebase to
+  render identically; otherwise a close fallback is substituted.
+- **Re-exporting** a file you imported will not be byte-identical to the
+  original, but preserves the structure and content faithfully.
+
+## Automating with the CLI
+
+Every import/export path above is also scriptable. See the
+[CLI reference](../developers/cli) for `docs export`, `docs import`,
+`slides export`, `slides import`, and the `sheets` cell import/export
+commands — useful for batch conversions and pipelines.

+# External Datasources
+
+A **datasource** connects a spreadsheet to an external PostgreSQL database. You
+write a SQL query and its results appear in a read-only tab, right next to your
+regular editable sheets.
+
+## Connect a database
+
+1. Click the **+** at the end of the tab bar and choose **New DataSource**.
+2. In the **Select DataSource** dialog, fill in the connection details:
+   - **Name** — a label for the connection
+   - **Host** and **Port** (defaults to `5432`)
+   - **Database**, **Username**, and **Password**
+   - **SSL** — toggle on if your database requires it
+3. Click **Test Connection** to confirm the credentials work, then save.
+
+A new tab is added with a database icon to distinguish it from sheet tabs.
+
+## Run a query
+
+The datasource tab has a SQL editor at the top and a results grid below it.
+
+1. Type a `SELECT` query — for example, `SELECT * FROM users LIMIT 100`.
+2. Click **Execute**, or press **⌘+Enter** / **Ctrl+Enter**.
+
+The results load into the grid below: the first row holds the column names and
+each following row is a record. Re-run the query with **Execute** whenever you
+want fresh data — results don't refresh automatically.
+
+::: tip
+Queries are capped at 10,000 rows and a 30-second runtime, so add a `LIMIT`
+clause when exploring large tables.
+:::
+
+## Working with results
+
+- The results grid is **read-only** — it reflects the database, so you can't
+  edit, sort, or filter the cells in place. Shape the data with SQL instead.
+- Reference query results from other tabs with formulas, just like any sheet,
+  to build summaries and dashboards on top of live data.
+
+## Good to know
+
+- Datasources connect to **PostgreSQL** databases.
+- The connection belongs to the person who created it. Collaborators can see the
+  query and its last results, but run their own connection to execute it.
+- Only the latest query for a tab is saved.

+# Import & Export
+
+Wafflebase reads and writes the file formats your team already uses, so you
+can bring existing work in and take finished work out. Nothing is locked to
+the platform.
+
+## At a glance
+
+| Product | Import | Export |
+|---------|--------|--------|
+| **Sheets** | Excel (`.xlsx`) | — *(CSV/JSON via [CLI](../developers/cli))* |
+| **Docs** | Word (`.docx`) | Word (`.docx`), PDF (`.pdf`) |
+| **Slides** | PowerPoint (`.pptx`) | PowerPoint (`.pptx`), PDF (`.pdf`) |
+
+Import always creates a **new** document; it never overwrites an open one.
+Export downloads a file from the document you are editing.
+
+## Importing files
+
+From your workspace, open the **New** menu and choose an import option:
+
+- **Import XLSX** — creates a new spreadsheet from an Excel workbook. Each
+  sheet in the workbook becomes a tab. Values, formulas, and basic cell
+  formatting are brought across.
+- **Import DOCX** — creates a new document from a Word file, mapping
+  paragraphs, headings, lists, tables, and inline formatting into the editor.
+- **Import PPTX** — creates a new deck from a PowerPoint file: slides,
+  text boxes, shapes, images, tables, and theme colors are converted to
+  native Wafflebase elements.
+
+Large files show a progress indicator while they are parsed and any embedded
+images are uploaded into your workspace.
+
+## Exporting files
+
+### Docs
+
+In the document editor, open the **Export** menu (the download icon in the
+header) and choose:
+
+- **Word (`.docx`)** — the full document, including tables and headers/footers.
+- **PDF (`.pdf`)** — a paginated, print-ready PDF that mirrors the on-screen
+  page layout.
+
+### Slides
+
+In the presentation editor, open the **Export** menu and choose:
+
+- **PowerPoint (`.pptx`)** — an editable deck with slides, shapes, text,
+  images, tables, and the theme preserved as DrawingML.
+- **PDF (`.pdf`)** — one slide per page, ready to share or print.
+
+### Sheets
+
+Spreadsheets export to CSV or JSON through the
+[command-line tool](../developers/cli) (`wafflebase sheets …`). A built-in
+download menu in the grid editor is on the roadmap.
+
+## Fidelity notes
+
+Wafflebase aims for a faithful round-trip, but the source formats are large
+and some constructs have no exact equivalent:
+
+- **PPTX/DOCX import is best-effort.** Common content — text, lists, tables,
+  shapes, images, and theme colors — converts cleanly. Rare or
+  application-specific features (embedded objects, macros, exotic effects) may
+  be simplified or dropped.
+- **Fonts** referenced by an imported file must be available in Wafflebase to
+  render identically; otherwise a close fallback is substituted.
+- **Re-exporting** a file you imported will not be byte-identical to the
+  original, but preserves the structure and content faithfully.
+
+## Automating with the CLI
+
+Every import/export path above is also scriptable. See the
+[CLI reference](../developers/cli) for `docs export`, `docs import`,
+`slides export`, `slides import`, and the `sheets` cell import/export
+commands — useful for batch conversions and pipelines.

+# External Datasources
+
+A **datasource** connects a spreadsheet to an external PostgreSQL database. You
+write a SQL query and its results appear in a read-only tab, right next to your
+regular editable sheets.
+
+## Connect a database
+
+1. Click the **+** at the end of the tab bar and choose **New DataSource**.
+2. In the **Select DataSource** dialog, fill in the connection details:
+   - **Name** — a label for the connection
+   - **Host** and **Port** (defaults to `5432`)
+   - **Database**, **Username**, and **Password**
+   - **SSL** — toggle on if your database requires it
+3. Click **Test Connection** to confirm the credentials work, then save.
+
+A new tab is added with a database icon to distinguish it from sheet tabs.
+
+## Run a query
+
+The datasource tab has a SQL editor at the top and a results grid below it.
+
+1. Type a `SELECT` query — for example, `SELECT * FROM users LIMIT 100`.
+2. Click **Execute**, or press **⌘+Enter** / **Ctrl+Enter**.
+
+The results load into the grid below: the first row holds the column names and
+each following row is a record. Re-run the query with **Execute** whenever you
+want fresh data — results don't refresh automatically.
+
+::: tip
+Queries are capped at 10,000 rows and a 30-second runtime, so add a `LIMIT`
+clause when exploring large tables.
+:::
+
+## Working with results
+
+- The results grid is **read-only** — it reflects the database, so you can't
+  edit, sort, or filter the cells in place. Shape the data with SQL instead.
+- Reference query results from other tabs with formulas, just like any sheet,
+  to build summaries and dashboards on top of live data.
+
+## Good to know
+
+- Datasources connect to **PostgreSQL** databases.
+- The connection belongs to the person who created it. Collaborators can see the
+  query and its last results, but run their own connection to execute it.
+- Only the latest query for a tab is saved.

samples.summary: New PPTX export fetches arbitrary, document-controlled image URLs with `credentials: "include"` and no scheme/host allowlist
samples.evidence:
`exportSlidesPptxAndDownload` passes every image element's `src` straight into `docsImageFetcher` (pptx-actions.ts:93-99), which resolves it via `resolveImageUrl` — that function deliberately preserves ANY absolute URL (`export-utils.ts:15`) — and then issues `fetch(resolved, { credentials: "include" })` (export-utils.ts:51).

The `src` is fully attacker-controllable: the v1 content endpoint validates only `id`/`type`/`frame` per element (`packages/backend/src/api/v1/docs-content.controller.ts:337-357`) and never inspects `data.src`, so any workspace member or API-key holder (or a collaborator driving a patched CRDT client on a shared deck) can store `data: { src: "https://attacker.example/beacon.png" }`.

Attack: attacker plants such an element in a shared deck; when a victim clicks Export → PowerPoint (slides-export-button.tsx), the victim's browser performs a credentialed GET to the attacker origin — leaking victim IP/UA/export timing, performing GET-side-effect CSRF against third-party or intranet origins with the victim's ambient cookies (no preflight for a simple GET, so the request is sent even when the response is CORS-blocked), and, when the attacker server returns permissive CORS headers, embedding arbitrary attacker bytes verbatim as a `ppt/media/` part in the victim's downloaded file. Same pattern exists in the pre-existing PDF/DOCX paths, but this change adds a third unguarded consumer and the PPTX one embeds the fetched bytes byte-for-byte rather than rasterising them.

samples.summary: No size or content-type validation on bytes fetched for PPTX media parts
samples.evidence: `await blob.arrayBuffer()` is called on an unbounded response and `mime` falls back to `blob.type || "image/png"`; `exportPptx` then writes those bytes as `ppt/media/imageN.<ext>` (packages/slides/src/export/pptx/index.ts:161-166). A hostile or oversized `src` (attacker-controlled, see the credentialed-fetch finding) can therefore exhaust the exporting tab's memory or place non-image content into the archive the victim then shares onward. verdict.reason: The finding is present exactly as described and reachable. `exportSlidesPptxAndDownload` (packages/frontend/src/app/slides/pptx-actions.ts:92-101) forwards every image element's `src` into `docsImageFetcher` with no filtering; `exportPptx` (packages/slides/src/export/pptx/index.ts:139-166) harvests `el.data.src` from all slides and calls `fetchImage` on each. `resolveImageUrl` (packages/frontend/src/app/docs/export-utils.ts:12-18) deliberately returns any absolute URL untouched, and `docsImageFetcher` (export-utils.ts:46-56) performs `fetch(resolved, { credentials: "include" })` — a credentialed request to a document-controlled origin. The `src` is attacker-controllable: `assertValidElement` (packages/backend/src/api/v1/docs-content.controller.ts:337-357) validates only `id`, `type`, and `frame` and never inspects `data`/`data.src`; a repo-wide grep found no scheme/host allowlist or src sanitiser anywhere. The path is user-reachable via the export menu (packages/frontend/src/app/slides/slides-export-button.tsx:107). No guard elsewhere makes it unreachable, so `already-guarded` and `not-present` are both ruled out. The issue is in the security lane (client-side SSRF / credentialed cross-origin fetch, victim IP-UA-timing leak, GET-side-effect CSRF with ambient cookies, and verbatim embedding of attacker bytes as a ppt/media part), so it is not out-of-scope. The only nuance is that a cross-origin response is normally CORS-blocked absent permissive headers, which limits the byte-embedding leg but does not stop the credentialed request from being sent (simple GET, no preflight) — consistent with the reviewer's `major` rating rather than critical.

finding.summary: New datasources doc advertises an SSL toggle, but the client disables TLS certificate verification (`rejectUnauthorized: false`)
finding.evidence: `packages/documentation/sheets/datasources.md` (added by this change) tells users to enable **SSL** "if your database requires it", presenting it as a protection. The implementation builds the pg client with `ssl: ds.sslEnabled ? { rejectUnauthorized: false } : false` (datasource.service.ts:204), so the server certificate is never validated — an on-path attacker between the Wafflebase backend and the customer database can transparently MITM the connection and capture the decrypted database username/password (decrypt() is called on the same line). The new documentation makes the false assurance user-facing. Pre-existing code, surfaced by the doc added here.

verdict.reason: Verified directly in the repository. datasource.service.ts:204 builds the pg Client with `ssl: ds.sslEnabled ? { rejectUnauthorized: false } : false`, so enabling SSL encrypts without validating the server certificate or hostname. The decrypted database credentials are supplied on the adjacent line (datasource.service.ts:203, `password: decrypt(ds.password)`), so an on-path attacker can present any self-signed cert, complete the handshake, and capture the plaintext DB username/password and all query traffic. I enumerated every call site of the client factory: createClient is invoked only at datasource.service.ts:115 (test-connection) and :138 (query execution), both routed through the same unverified config; there is no CA option, checkServerIdentity, or env override anywhere in packages/backend/src that could restore verification (grep for sslEnabled/new Client( shows only DTO boolean validation at datasource.dto.ts:41,83 and persistence at :52,:93). The documentation claim also holds: packages/documentation/sheets/datasources.md:14 presents `**SSL** — toggle on if your database requires it` as the connection-security control with no caveat, making the false assurance user-facing. This sits squarely in the Security lane (weakened/absent certificate verification plus sensitive credential exposure), so no refutation ground applies: not not-present (both cited lines read verbatim), not already-guarded (no verification path exists), not out-of-scope. Pre-existing status is irrelevant per the instructions, since a defect at an untouched location is still a defect. Major severity is appropriate: a clear cryptographic weakness requiring an on-path position rather than a directly reachable bypass.

finding.summary: New datasources doc promises read-only query execution, enforced only by a keyword denylist that is bypassable
finding.evidence: `sheets/datasources.md` (added here) states the results grid is read-only and implies queries are read-only. Enforcement is a regex denylist (`INSERT|UPDATE|DELETE|DROP|ALTER|CREATE|TRUNCATE|GRANT|REVOKE|EXEC|EXECUTE`) plus a first-token check for SELECT/WITH (sql-validator.ts:38-57). `SELECT ... INTO newtable FROM t` starts with SELECT and contains no denylisted keyword, so it passes and writes to the target database; the semicolon splitter strips only single-quoted strings (line 60), so dollar-quoted bodies (`$$ ... ; ... $$`) also evade the multi-statement check. Any workspace member — not just the datasource owner, see datasource.controller.ts:133-145 where only `assertMember` is required — can send these through `POST /datasources/:id/query` using credentials they never possessed. Pre-existing code newly advertised by this change; I did not execute a live bypass, hence low confidence.

verdict.reason: Code is present exactly as described. sql-validator.ts:1-13 defines the keyword denylist; :38-44 is the first-token SELECT/WITH check; :48-57 the \bKEYWORD\b loop; :60-61 the semicolon splitter that strips only single-quoted strings (so dollar-quoted bodies are unhandled). datasource.service.ts:128-131 is the sole enforcement before executing user SQL at :150-152, and no read-only transaction or read-only role is used (createClient :190-208). The denylist is provably incomplete: \bEXEC\b does not match identifiers like dblink_exec, and side-effecting calls (setval, nextval, pg_terminate_backend, lo_import, user-defined writing functions) pass all checks and execute fine inside the SELECT * FROM (...) AS _q wrapper. The reviewer's specific SELECT ... INTO example is probably neutralized by that subquery wrapping (Postgres rejects SELECT INTO in a sub-select), but that refutes one illustration, not the defect. The authorization half is fully accurate: datasource.controller.ts:139-144 requires only assertMember (workspace.service.ts:167) before executing with the owner's decrypted credentials (datasource.service.ts:203), and this is the only production call site of executeQuery — so any workspace member gets arbitrary SQL execution under credentials they never held, directly contradicting the repo's own documented model at sheets/datasources.md:45-46. In-lane (unsafe input handling / weakened access control), reachable, real.
